terra.problem: The snooze-button joke makes persistent sin into a trivial habit.
The explanation repeats that the verse gives a reason without adding anything to the quoted reason.
“Wrong spot” uses “wrong” about the baker’s answer.
“Ten chariots, and that's all that was left” overlooks the horsemen and foot soldiers named in the verse.
“Ten chariots is all that was left to him” overlooks the horsemen and foot soldiers named in the verse.
The claim that Samaria was Israel’s capital is not stated in this passage and needs an outside reference.
The claim that Jerusalem was the city of Judah’s kings is not stated in this passage and needs an outside reference.
“Jehoash and Joash are two different kings” treats the names as belonging to distinct people generally. Both names are also used for the same king of Israel (2 Kings 13:10; 14:1).
The text says the king wept over Elisha, not that he stood.
The comparison implies Elisha was steadying the king’s hands. The text does not give that reason for placing his hands on them.
The text says the arrow was shot through the east window and signified victory over Aram; it does not say it was aimed at Aram.
The explanation mechanically repeats “victory” without offering much beyond the quote.
“The promise stopped with him” suggests the promise ceased, although Elisha says the king will strike Aram three times.
The text does not say the Israelites lacked time to do anything else.
The text does not say nobody expected the revival. It also does not say the burial party or raiders ran; marking that as a guess does not make it a stated event.
The verse gives God’s covenant as the reason, but it does not make the broader claim that it was not anything Israel did.
